summary.text: Since the product is not \(1\), the associated-prime set is nonempty, so one may choose its maximum \(m\). The bound \(m\le M/2\) gives \(M-m\ge2\), and any prime factor that could witness its compositeness would be at most \(\sqrt M\) and force \(m\equiv M\pmod q\), contradicting the defining modular avoidance condition; hence \(M-m\) and \(m\) form the required prime partition.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\) denote the integer square root of a natural number \(M\). For \(M>0\), define \(GB(M)\) to be the finite set of natural numbers \(p\) satisfying
\[
 p\text{ is prime},\qquad \lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor<p\leq \left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor,
\]
and
\[
 p\not\equiv M\pmod q
 \quad\text{for every prime }q\leq \lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor.
\]
For \(M=0\), set \(GB(0)=\varnothing\). This is the set used in the definition of the sequence, and it is finite because all its elements are at most \(M/2\).

The modular condition is the usual Goldbach-associated condition from the sequence description. Indeed, if \(p>\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\) and \(q\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\) is prime, then \(q<p\), so the prime \(q\) cannot divide the prime \(p\). Consequently
\[
 q\nmid p(p-M)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q\nmid(p-M)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\not\equiv M\pmod q.
\]
Thus the modular formulation and the divisibility formulation define the same associated primes.

For \(n\in\mathbb N\), the sequence term in question is
\[
 a(n)=\prod_{p\in GB(2n)}p,
\]
with the exceptional zero case also assigned the value \(1\). In particular, when \(n\geq3\), we have \(2n\ne0\), so this displayed product is exactly the definition of \(a(n)\).

We first prove the central fact about associated primes.

**Lemma.** If \(M>0\) and \(p\in GB(M)\), then \(M-p\) is prime.

**Proof of the lemma.** Membership of \(p\) in \(GB(M)\) gives three facts that will be used repeatedly:

1. \(p\) is prime;
2. \(p\leq M/2\);
3. for every prime \(q\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\), one has \(p\not\equiv M\pmod q\).

Since \(p\leq M/2\), we have \(2p\leq M\), and hence
\[
 p\leq M-p.
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, \(p\geq2\). It follows that
\[
 M-p\geq p\geq2.
\]
We now show that \(M-p\) has no divisor between \(2\) and its integer square root. Suppose, for a contradiction, that a natural number \(d\) satisfies
\[
 2\leq d\leq\lfloor\sqrt{M-p}\rfloor
 \quad\text{and}\quad d\mid M-p.
\]
Since \(d>1\), some prime \(q\) divides \(d\). Divisibility is transitive, so \(q\mid M-p\). Moreover, a positive divisor cannot exceed the number it divides, and therefore
\[
 q\leq d\leq\lfloor\sqrt{M-p}\rfloor.
\]
We also have \(M-p\leq M\). Monotonicity of the integer square root consequently gives
\[
 \lfloor\sqrt{M-p}\rfloor\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor,
\]
so \(q\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\).

On the other hand, \(q\mid M-p\) says exactly that \(M\equiv p\pmod q\), or equivalently
\[
 p\bmod q=M\bmod q.
\]
This contradicts the defining avoidance condition for \(p\in GB(M)\), because \(q\) is prime and \(q\leq\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor\). Thus no such \(d\) exists.

A natural number at least \(2\) is prime if and only if it has no divisor \(d\) with
\(2\leq d\leq\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor\): if a composite number \(N\) is written as a product of two factors greater than \(1\), at least one factor is at most \(\sqrt N\). Applying this criterion to \(N=M-p\), the preceding argument proves that \(M-p\) is prime. This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

We next establish the local claim. Fix \(n\geq3\) and suppose that \(a(n)\ne1\). Put
\[
 M=2n,
 \qquad S=GB(M).
\]
Since \(n\geq3\), \(M\ne0\), and hence
\[
 a(n)=\prod_{p\in S}p.
\]
The set \(S\) cannot be empty. Indeed, the product over an empty set is \(1\), whereas its product here is \(a(n)\ne1\). Thus \(S\) is a nonempty finite set.

Every nonempty finite set of natural numbers has a greatest element. Let
\[
 m=\max S.
\]
Then
\[
 m\in S
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 k\leq m\quad\text{for every }k\in S.
\]
This proves both the asserted nonemptiness of \(GB(2n)\) and the asserted existence and maximality of \(m\).

Because \(m\in GB(M)\), the definition gives that \(m\) is prime and that
\[
 m\leq M/2\leq M.
\]
The lemma, applied to \(M\) and \(m\), says that \(M-m\) is prime as well. Since \(m\leq M\), subtraction in the natural numbers satisfies
\[
 (M-m)+m=M.
\]
Recalling that \(M=2n\), we obtain
\[
 2n=(2n-m)+m,
\]
where both \(2n-m\) and \(m\) are prime. Therefore \((2n-m,m)\) is a Goldbach partition of \(2n\). In particular, the chosen \(m\) is not merely an associated prime but the maximum associated prime, exactly as claimed.

Finally, assume the global hypothesis
\[
 a(k)\ne1\qquad\text{for every }k\geq3.
\]
To prove Goldbach’s conjecture in the formulation at issue, take an arbitrary \(n\geq3\). The hypothesis gives \(a(n)\ne1\). Applying the local argument just proved, the finite set \(GB(2n)\) is nonempty; if \(m=\max GB(2n)\), then both \(m\) and \(2n-m\) are prime and
\[
 2n=(2n-m)+m.
\]
Thus every even number \(2n\) with \(n\geq3\) is a sum of two primes. This is the stated Goldbach conjecture, and the same construction simultaneously supplies the claimed maximum \(m\) and its associated Goldbach partition.
